title: A scheduler that lives inside the process
description: A recurring query normally means an external scheduler and a shell wrapper around the CLI. Cronjob moves the schedule inside the database instead: register SQL against a [cron expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron) and DuckDB runs it itself. The catch is the scope: schedules live in memory inside the running DuckDB process. When the process exits, every job is forgotten. Best fit when DuckDB is already a long-running service (a server, a daemon, an analytics worker), not a CLI you start and stop.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: Cronjob turns a long-running DuckDB process into its own task scheduler. Registering a query records an entry in an in-memory job table; a background thread owned by the database wakes when the next job is due and runs its SQL on a fresh connection to the same database. There is no separate process, no daemon, and nothing on disk — the scheduler *is* the DuckDB process.

bulletPoints.label: One background thread per database
bulletPoints.description: Each database that loads the extension gets its own scheduler thread, which sleeps until the next job is due, runs every due job, and records the outcome (status, last run time, last result or error message) in the job table. It is stopped and joined when the database closes. The introspection table surfaces all of that so you can monitor schedules from SQL like any other relation.

bulletPoints.label: Six-field cron expressions
bulletPoints.description: Schedules use the six-field form `second minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week` — one more field than POSIX, giving second-level resolution, evaluated in UTC. The standard `*`, `?`, `,`, `-`, `/` operators and `MON`–`SUN` weekday names all work. [crontab.guru](https://crontab.guru/) is handy for sanity-checking, but note it parses the five-field POSIX form, so the leading `seconds` field here is an extension.

bulletPoints.label: Same database, fresh connection
bulletPoints.description: A scheduled query runs on a new connection to the database the extension was loaded into, so it sees the same tables, attached databases and persistent secrets, and is subject to the same database-wide settings. Session state does not carry over: `SET` variables, temporary tables and temporary secrets from the registering session are not visible. Register against an in-memory database and the schedule disappears when that database does, even before process exit.

bulletPoints.label: Sequential, one job at a time
bulletPoints.description: The scheduler thread runs due jobs one after another. A job never overlaps itself, and fire times missed while a run was in progress are skipped, not replayed. A slow job also delays the other jobs in the same database until it finishes.

sections.title: Production caveats
sections.description: The scheduler's strength — living inside the process — is also the source of every limitation. Internalize these before scheduling anything important.

bulletPoints.label: Schedules die with the process
bulletPoints.description: This is the central caveat. A `kill -9`, a deploy, an OOM, or a clean shutdown all wipe the in-memory registry — there is no WAL entry, no on-disk table, and no resume. If the work must happen on a wall-clock cadence regardless of process state, drive the run from an external orchestrator (system [`cron(8)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/cron.8.html), [`systemd` timers](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.timer.html), [Kubernetes CronJob](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/)) and have *that* invoke DuckDB.

bulletPoints.label: No multi-process coordination
bulletPoints.description: Two DuckDB processes that both load Cronjob and register the same job will both run it. There is no leader election and no lease — pick one process to own the schedule, or de-duplicate downstream.

bulletPoints.label: Errors are recorded, not retried
bulletPoints.description: A failed query writes its error message into the job's last-result column. The extension does not retry, back off, or alert — wrap the scheduled query in its own error-reporting logic (write to an audit table, fire a webhook) if you need notification.

bulletPoints.label: Long-running queries delay other jobs
bulletPoints.description: Jobs share one scheduler thread per database, so a query that overruns delays its own next run and every other job due behind it. Schedule with headroom, or split heavy work so no single run can starve the cadence.

bulletPoints.label: Experimental status
bulletPoints.description: Marked experimental upstream. The function surface is small and stable in spirit, but pin a known-good extension version in production until it's promoted.
